questions.question: A company runs a single-instance relational database on Amazon RDS and needs more capacity. The application is not distributed, and the team wants the simplest change. Which scaling approach fits best?
options: Scale vertically by moving to a larger RDS instance class
Scale horizontally by adding more RDS instances behind a load balancer
Run the database across multiple Availability Zones for extra capacity
Add an Auto Scaling Group to the database tier
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling increases the size of the instance and is the typical choice for non-distributed systems such as a database; RDS is named as a service that scales vertically. Adding more RDS instances behind a load balancer is horizontal scaling that changes the architecture rather than resizing. Multi-AZ gives resilience, not more capacity for the primary. Auto Scaling Groups manage EC2 instance counts, not RDS instance size.

questions.question: Which statement best describes horizontal scalability as defined for this exam?
options: It increases the size of a single instance so it can process more work
It increases the number of instances or systems and implies a distributed system
It places a standby copy of the workload in a second Availability Zone
It raises the vCPU count of one instance until the hardware limit is reached
questions.explanation: Horizontal scalability means increasing the number of instances or systems, which implies a distributed system and equals elasticity. Increasing instance size or vCPU count is vertical scaling. Placing a standby in a second AZ is passive high availability, not horizontal scaling.

questions.question: Why does horizontally scaling an application change its architecture more than vertically scaling it?
options: Because horizontal scaling requires a database instead of EC2 instances
Because horizontal scaling is limited by the maximum instance size
Because horizontal scaling implies a distributed system spread over multiple instances
Because horizontal scaling requires all instances in a single Availability Zone
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling adds instances and therefore produces a distributed system, which is why it is common for web and modern applications. It does not require a database, is not limited by instance size (that is a vertical constraint), and does not force a single AZ.

questions.question: An application must survive the loss of a data center. What does high availability require according to this section?
options: Running the application on a larger instance type in the same data center
Running the application in at least two data centers, that is, Availability Zones
Running the application on more instances within the same Availability Zone
Running the application only in a second Region with no local deployment
questions.explanation: High availability means running the application or system in at least two data centers (equal to Availability Zones) so a data center loss can be survived. A larger instance does not help if the data center is lost, more instances in one AZ are still lost together, and the section defines HA in terms of at least two AZs.

questions.question: A solutions architect keeps a database on RDS with Multi AZ enabled. The primary serves all traffic and the second AZ copy exists for failover. Which description fits this design?
options: Active high availability, because both copies serve read and write traffic
Horizontal scaling, because there are now two database instances
Passive high availability, because the standby exists for failover rather than serving traffic
Vertical scaling, because the database engine runs on a larger instance
questions.explanation: The section names RDS Multi AZ as the example of passive high availability, where a second copy exists for failover. The standby is not serving traffic, so it is not active HA; having two copies for failover is not horizontal scaling for capacity; and instance size is unrelated to this design.

questions.question: A web application runs on several EC2 instances spread across multiple Availability Zones, all actively serving requests behind a load balancer. Which statement about this design is correct?
options: This is active high availability, because the workload runs on multiple instances across AZs
This is passive high availability, because one instance acts as a standby
This is vertical scaling, because each instance was resized
This delivers high availability but no scalability
questions.explanation: Running the workload actively on several instances across AZs is active high availability, which the section says goes hand in hand with horizontal scaling. Passive HA would keep a standby rather than serving traffic, vertical scaling changes instance size, and horizontal scaling across instances also provides scalability.

questions.question: Which range correctly describes EC2 vertical scaling as presented in this section?
options: From t2.micro to t2.large, spanning 1 GB to 8 GB of RAM
From t2.nano with 0.5 GB of RAM and 1 vCPU to u-12tb1.metal with 12.3 TB of RAM and 448 vCPUs
From m5.large to m5.24xlarge within the same instance family
From a single instance to an Auto Scaling Group of instances
questions.explanation: The section states EC2 vertical scaling goes from t2.nano (0.5 GB RAM, 1 vCPU) to u-12tb1.metal (12.3 TB RAM, 448 vCPUs). The t2.micro to t2.large pair is the conceptual example of scaling one size up, not the stated range; the m5 family span is not the cited range; and moving to an Auto Scaling Group is horizontal scaling.

questions.question: A team adds an Auto Scaling Group so that EC2 capacity grows during peak traffic and shrinks afterwards. Which pair of terms matches this action?
options: Scale up to add instances and scale down to remove them
Scale out to add instances and scale in to remove instances
Scale out to resize instances and scale in to revert the size
Scale up to resize instances and scale out to remove instances
questions.explanation: On EC2, horizontal scaling changes the number of instances via the Auto Scaling Group, called scale out and scale in. Scale up and scale down refer to changing instance size, so the options that attach resizing to out/in or out to resizing are wrong.
questions.keyTopic: ASG scale out and scale in

questions.question: A company wants its EC2 web tier to keep serving users if one Availability Zone becomes unavailable. The tier already uses an Auto Scaling Group and a Load Balancer in a single AZ. What change best meets the requirement?
options: Increase the instance size of the EC2 instances in the existing AZ
Configure the Auto Scaling Group to span multiple AZs and make the Load Balancer multi-AZ
Increase the maximum size of the Auto Scaling Group within the same AZ
Replace the Load Balancer with a larger instance type running the application
questions.explanation: For EC2 the high availability pattern is ASG multi AZ plus Load Balancer multi AZ, so the application survives an AZ loss. Resizing instances or raising the ASG maximum keeps all capacity in one AZ, which does not survive that AZ's loss. Replacing the load balancer with one larger instance concentrates risk rather than spreading it across AZs.
